evidence.claim: In the 1860s, anglers from eastern cities discovered brook trout weighing 10 to 12 pounds in the region. As word spread, sportsmen and their families began returning annually, traveling by train, buckboard and steamship.
evidence.quote: By the 1860s, fishermen from cities along the eastern seaboard discovered 10 to 12 lbs brook trout swimming in this region’s pristine waters.

evidence.claim: As word spread, sportsmen and their families began returning annually, traveling by train, buckboard and steamship.
evidence.quote: large numbers of sportsmen and their families began to journey to the region annually. Travelling by trains, buckboards, and steamships

evidence.claim: As word spread, sportsmen and their families began returning annually, traveling by train, buckboard and steamship.
evidence.quote: As word began to spread about the region’s unparalleled fishing and rugged beauty, large numbers of sportsmen and their families began to journey to the region annually.

evidence.claim: Travel here changed with the vehicles that brought visitors. The Phillips and Rangeley Railroad opened in 1891, carrying timber to market and bringing tourists from eastern cities.
evidence.quote: The Phillips and Rangeley Railroad, a narrow gauge common carrier, opened in 1891, becoming part of the Sandy River and Rangeley Lakes Railroad in 1908. Timber and other goods were shipped to markets, and tourists arrived from Boston; Hartford; New York City; and Philadelphia.

evidence.claim: With the railroad’s end, the automobile and an expanding road network helped shift vacations toward personal camps. The big hotels declined; the Rangeley Lake House was demolished in 1958.
evidence.quote: The big hotels would decline, however, with the end of the railroad and invention of the automobile and proliferation of roads leading to vacationers building personal camps. In 1958, The Rangeley Lake House was razed.

evidence.claim: Begin north of Byron on Route 17 and travel north toward Oquossoc.
evidence.quote: The byway begins just north of Byron on state route 17. Visitors will cross the Appalachian Trail as they travel north to Oquossoc.

evidence.claim: Height of Land gives a view across the lakes region to the mountains beyond, beside the Appalachian Trail.
evidence.quote: Height of Land, a large view area with an expansive look at the sprawling Rangeley Lakes region and the mountains beyond. This area borders the Appalachian trail.

evidence.claim: From Oquossoc, follow the lake east toward Rangeley, then turn south on Route 4 to Smalls Falls. The Appalachian Trail crosses both Routes 17 and 4.
evidence.quote: The byway then heads east on state route 16 toward Rangeley, paralleling the lake most of the way. From Rangeley, the byway goes south on state route 4 to Smalls Falls.

evidence.claim: From Oquossoc, follow the lake east toward Rangeley, then turn south on Route 4 to Smalls Falls. The Appalachian Trail crosses both Routes 17 and 4.
evidence.quote: the famous Appalachian Trail, which crosses both Routes 4 and 17

evidence.claim: Height of Land puts the Rangeley Lakes region and the mountains beyond into one view. The overlook lies on the Route 17 portion of the byway, before Oquossoc when traveling north, and borders the Appalachian Trail.
evidence.quote: Begin your route just north of Houghton on Maine Route 17, which you will follow north.

evidence.quote: Soon after you begin, make a stop at the Height of Land, a large view area with an expansive look at the sprawling Rangeley Lakes region and the mountains beyond.

evidence.claim: Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust places its Byway Ambassadors here on summer weekends. Their work includes helping visitors find trails and places to look for moose.
evidence.quote: Are you looking for trails or where to see a moose? Our nationally acclaimed Byway Ambassadors will help you find your unique place in the Rangley Lakes Region.

evidence.claim: A ten-mile road was part of Squire James Rangeley’s plan for an estate here. Arriving in 1825, he tried to establish an English system of landlords and tenants, built a sawmill, gristmill and two-story mansion, and connected his property to the outside world by road.
evidence.quote: He arrived in 1825 to establish an estate based on the English system of landlord and tenants, also giving extensive land to settlers.

evidence.claim: A ten-mile road was part of Squire James Rangeley’s plan for an estate here. Arriving in 1825, he tried to establish an English system of landlords and tenants, built a sawmill, gristmill and two-story mansion, and connected his property to the outside world by road.
evidence.quote: He built a sawmill, a gristmill, a two-story mansion, and a ten-mile (16 km) road to connect his property with the rest of the world.

evidence.claim: He stayed 15 years before selling and moving to Portland. Logging became a principal industry, with steamboats towing log booms across the lakes before river drives carried them onward.
evidence.quote: Rangeley resided here for 15 years, then sold the property and moved to Portland.

evidence.claim: He stayed 15 years before selling and moving to Portland. Logging became a principal industry, with steamboats towing log booms across the lakes before river drives carried them onward.
evidence.quote: Farms produced hay, wheat, oats, barley and potatoes, with cattle grazing the hills.

evidence.claim: He stayed 15 years before selling and moving to Portland. Logging became a principal industry, with steamboats towing log booms across the lakes before river drives carried them onward.
evidence.quote: Logging became a principal industry, with booms of logs towed by steamboat across the Rangeley lakes, then guided down rivers in log drives.

evidence.claim: A sign in town marks another kind of position: halfway between the Equator and North Pole.
evidence.quote: A sign in town notes that Rangeley is halfway between the Equator and North Pole.

evidence.claim: Smalls Falls breaks the Sandy River’s descent into four steps, with pools separating them. Together the waterfalls and cascades drop 54 feet. From the top, the sequence is a 12-foot slide and horsetail, a 25-foot segmented waterfall, a 14-foot horsetail and a three-foot cascade.
evidence.quote: It totals 54 feet (16 m) in height, and consists of (from top to bottom) a 12-foot slide/horsetail, a 25-foot segmented waterfall, a 14-foot horsetail, and a 3-foot cascade, separated by pools.

evidence.claim: The falls lie in Township E in western Franklin County. A Route 4 rest area provides access and includes parking and picnic tables.
evidence.quote: Smalls Falls, a waterfall in Maine, is a series of waterfalls and cascades on the Sandy River in Township E, West Central Franklin, Maine, in the United States.

evidence.claim: The falls lie in Township E in western Franklin County. A Route 4 rest area provides access and includes parking and picnic tables.
evidence.quote: A rest area on Maine Route 4 provides access to the falls; the rest area includes pit toilets, parking and picnic tables.

evidence.claim: Pools separate the four drops of Smalls Falls.
evidence.quote: a 12-foot slide/horsetail, a 25-foot segmented waterfall, a 14-foot horsetail, and a 3-foot cascade, separated by pools.

flags: Cache gives 52 miles (Foundation) versus 35.6 miles (archived FHWA); total distance omitted. Conserved-land acreage also differs in scope and is omitted.
Foundation directions say east from Oquossoc to Rangeley, but its itinerary says west; use east, corroborated by village geography.
No construction or campaign history for the designated corridor is supplied; transport history explains the road-era change without identifying the earlier estate road with this byway.
Height of Land and Smalls Falls kept short because stop-specific evidence is limited. Rangeley’s existing coordinate is preserved as required but represents the town, not the village center.
Archived FHWA driving time is attributed as historical guidance, not a current travel-time measurement.
The current draft named north of Byron as the start of Route 17 itself. Cache 01 defines it as the byway start; cache 14 places the highway’s start in Oquossoc. Copy distinguishes the two.
